strings.name: Julia Gillard
strings.role: Former Australian prime minister and Chair of Wellcome's Board of Governors
strings.summary: Julia Gillard served as Australia's first woman prime minister from 2010 to 2013, after holding the deputy premiership and education and other portfolios. She subsequently turned to global education, women's leadership and public health. A former chair of the Global Partnership for Education, she chairs Wellcome's Board of Governors and is founding chair of the Global Institute for Women's Leadership.
strings.coverageNote: Information checked through 18 November 2026. Recent activity is supported by the University of Melbourne's 20 October report of her address. Party leadership changes and departure from the premiership are dated separately. Her chairmanships of Beyond Blue and the Global Partnership for Education are past roles.
strings.influence.rationale: Australia's first woman prime minister, she later promoted global education cooperation and women's leadership, with influence on public policy across countries.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birth and education
strings.facts.f1.value: Born on 29 September 1961 in Barry, Wales, United Kingdom; migrated to Australia with her family in 1966. The National Archives records a University of Melbourne law degree in 1986 and arts degree in 1989.
strings.facts.f2.label: Changes in charitable roles
strings.facts.f2.value: Chaired the Global Partnership for Education board from 2014 to 2021 and Beyond Blue from 2017 to 2023. After stepping down at the end of 2023, she remained a Beyond Blue patron, a role distinct from board leadership.
strings.highlights.h1.title: Minority government and reform agenda
strings.highlights.h1.text: After the 2010 election produced a hung parliament, she secured Greens and independent support for a minority government and pursued carbon pricing, school-funding and disability-support reforms. Legislation, implementation and lasting outcomes require separate assessment. Internal party leadership disputes ultimately led to her departure in 2013.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Public work in education, gender and health
strings.highlights.h2.text: After leaving office, she continued public work through education partnerships, women's leadership research and governance of a research charity. In October 2026 she also joined Hakluyt's international advisory board, an advisory position rather than chairmanship of the firm or an Australian government office.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Discusses climate and health leadership in Melbourne
strings.timeline.t1.text: The University of Melbourne reported that she had delivered the Climate CATCH Lab annual oration and participated in a preceding roundtable, urging cooperation among government, research and communities. This entry uses the report's publication date, not a verified same-day event date. Advocacy is not evidence of already achieved health improvements.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Becomes Chair of Wellcome's Board of Governors
strings.timeline.t2.text: Succeeded Eliza Manningham-Buller in overseeing the research charity's governance. The appointment was announced in May 2020 and took effect in April 2021. The chair is distinct from the executive leadership responsible for daily management.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Helps establish the Global Institute for Women's Leadership
strings.timeline.t3.text: King's College London announced the institute with Gillard as founding chair, using research, practice and advocacy to examine women's underrepresentation and bias in leadership. The April establishment announcement and subsequent events are recorded separately.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Appointed chair of the Global Partnership for Education
strings.timeline.t4.text: The organisation announced her appointment as board chair to advance cooperation on education funding and policy. She served until 2021. Old biographies should not make this a current role, and fundraising targets are neither personal donations nor verified numbers of children enrolled.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Delivers speech against misogyny and sexism
strings.timeline.t5.text: During a House of Representatives debate concerning the Speaker, she responded to opposition leader Tony Abbott and criticised sexism. The widely circulated speech became an important text in discussions of women's political leadership. Archival inclusion and later polls are not new legislation enacted on the speech date.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Becomes Australia's first woman prime minister
strings.timeline.t6.text: Elected leader by the parliamentary Labor Party and sworn in the same day, rather than directly elected prime minister in a nationwide ballot. She lost a party leadership vote to Kevin Rudd on 26 June 2013; her resignation as prime minister took effect on 27 June. The dates are distinct.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Becomes deputy prime minister and minister
strings.timeline.t7.text: Served under Kevin Rudd as deputy prime minister and held education, employment and workplace relations, and social inclusion portfolios. Her deputy premiership ended on 24 June 2010, while the ministerial portfolios ended on 28 June.
strings.timeline.t8.title: First elected to the federal House of Representatives
strings.timeline.t8.text: Entered parliament for Lalor in Victoria, serving until 5 August 2013. She had worked as a solicitor and chief of staff to Victorian opposition leader John Brumby. Brumby was not yet premier during that employment.
